title: "To the discerning, all is suffering" (2.15–2.17)
hook: the gloomiest-sounding line in the sutras turns out to be about sensitivity, and about the pain that hasn't come yet
tomorrow: The purpose of the world: experience and liberation

segments.voice: Yesterday: karmashaya, the storehouse. Action leaves a seed, and the afflictions are the husk that lets it sprout. Today, a line that sounds gloomy at first.

An eyelash falls onto your cheek. You don't notice it all afternoon. The same eyelash lands in your eye, and suddenly you can't read, can't talk, can't think of anything else. Same eyelash. Different place. Read fast, today's sutra sounds like Patanjali hated life. But the old commentary explains it with a picture very like this one, the eye and a tiny thread, and once you see it, the line stops sounding like despair. It starts sounding like a diagnosis.
screen: `AN EYELASH ON YOUR CHEEK.` → `THE SAME EYELASH IN YOUR EYE.` → `NOT DESPAIR. A DIAGNOSIS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.15 says: to the discerning, all is suffering. Duhkha. The one who sees clearly, the vivekin, finds pain even in pleasure, and Patanjali gives four reasons. Change: the sweet thing is already ending. Anxiety: while you have it, you fear losing it. Impressions: it leaves a groove that wants more. And the three qualities of nature, always pulling against each other, so nothing stays settled. The commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, explains who the discerning person is. Most people, it says, are like the rest of the body: a thread of wool lands on an arm or a leg and nothing is felt. The discerning person is like the eyeball. The same thread, and it hurts. So the line isn't a mood. It's about becoming sensitive enough to feel what was always there. Then the turn. Sutra 2.16 is three words in Sanskrit: heyam duhkham anagatam. The suffering not yet come is to be avoided. The past is done. The present is already being lived. Only the future is still open, and that is where practice works. And 2.17 names the cause: the joining of the seer and the seen. The pure awareness that watches, and everything it watches, mind included, tangled until awareness mistakes itself for what it sees. The commentary notices that this follows the order of medicine: the disease, its cause, the cure, the remedy. Today, the first two.
screen: `TO THE DISCERNING, ALL IS SUFFERING.` · `THE LIMB AND THE EYEBALL.` · `AVOID THE PAIN NOT YET COME.` · `THE CAUSE: SEER JOINED TO SEEN.` · then, large: `THE SEEN AND THE SEER.`

segments.voice: Notice one sensation, the weight of your hands, a sound in the room, an itch: that's the seen. Then notice that something is noticing it, and feel the difference between the sound and the hearing of it. When a thought comes, let it join the seen, one more thing in the room, and rest as the one watching.
Duhkha, suffering, pain, unease, the opposite of ease. Not a mood but a sensitivity, like the eye that feels the thread, and a turn toward the pain that hasn't come yet.
Your line: the seen and the seer. The disease and its cause have names now; the cure is coming. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 454 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PURPOSE OF THE WORLD.`

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often present 2.15–2.17 as a medical outline, the illness and its cause, followed later by the cure and the remedy, and students reflect on it in study and in meditation on the difference between awareness and what it is aware of.

fork.setup: you're the discerning one, and you can feel the pain inside even pleasant things. which pain does Patanjali say to work on?
options: the pain from the past, by going over it again.
the pain you're in right now, by fighting it.
the pain that hasn't come yet.
fork.reveal: 2.16: the suffering not yet come is to be avoided. the past is spent and the present is already being lived; the future is where practice can still act.

original.note: Sanskrit duḥkha: pain, suffering, unease; the opposite of sukha, ease.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga says life is suffering, so be gloomy.
what it means: the clear-seeing person feels the pain inside even pleasure, and works to prevent the pain still to come.
what a scholar hears: four reasons in 2.15 (change, anxiety, impressions, the gunas' conflict); the commentary's eyeball simile; and a disease, cause, cure, remedy outline borrowed from medicine.

chat.says: Patanjali says all is suffering? That sounds so depressing.
options: It's a diagnosis: the eye feels the thread, and pain not yet come can be avoided.
It means life is meant to be endured, and nothing in it can ever change.
It means only the unwise suffer; once you're discerning, nothing hurts again.
chat.meaning: The commentary compares the discerning to an eyeball that feels a thread other limbs ignore. And 2.16 says suffering not yet come is to be avoided.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): the teach attributed a 'palm of the hand' to the Yoga Bhashya, which contrasts the eyeball with the other limbs; teach, screen head and match pair now say 'the rest of the body / other limbs'. The hook no longer claims the eyelash is 'exactly' the commentary's picture.
The four reasons in 2.15: parinama (change), tapa (anxiety/torment), samskara (impressions), guna-vritti-virodha (conflict of the gunas' movements). Confirm renderings.
The eyeball simile (the wise like an eyeball, others like other limbs; a wool thread) is attributed to the Yoga Bhashya on 2.15; the 'palm' is a simplification of 'other limbs'. Confirm.
Medical fourfold (disease, cause, health, remedy) attributed to the Bhashya; confirm placement (on 2.15).
